attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post assessing his 2022 essay. They are not quoted from anyone else.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'I think it is fair to say', the Deep Research concession and the 'most other respects' scope. It is a retrospective self-assessment, so observation is a defensible kind, but the overall judgment is evaluative and has no measure.

contract.note: The contract correctly declines to invent a weighting rule for 'most other respects' or a threshold for 'bang on'. Any overall verdict would rest on criteria the speaker never gave.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own launch disclosure (2025-02-02) admits reliability limits in Deep Research. It touches one theme only and cannot grade the aggregate self-assessment.

reviews.rationale: This is Marcus's qualified overall judgment that his essay was right 'in most other respects'. It names no set of respects, no weighting and no accuracy standard, so it cannot be tested as a whole. Individual themes could be checked separately, but their results would not settle the aggregate claim. The one evidence item is context only.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence. 'Apparently' signals that he is relaying second-hand reports, but he wrote and endorsed the statement.

semantics.note: The 'apparently' qualifier is kept. 'A bunch' becomes 'many', a slight firming that does not change the result. 'Apparently' marks an evidential, hedged allegation rather than a firm assertion.

contract.note: The contract rightly refuses to turn a hedged allegation of unspecified size into a binary claim. The report is not identified, and a scoring standard would have to be invented.

reviews.rationale: The allegation is hedged with 'apparently' and quantified only as 'a bunch'. Under the policy, hedged language is not scored. Separately, the packet neither identifies the specific tariff report nor contains an audit of its numbers, so even the underlying factual claim could not be checked.
